topic: Olympic art competitions 1912-1948 (Coubertin, Winans, Hajós, Copley)

slides.title: For 36 years, the Olympics gave medals for art.
slides.accent: Then the artists were too good.

slides.kicker: The founder had a bigger dream.
slides.body:
Pierre de Coubertin, who revived the modern Olympics, believed sport and art belonged together.

From 1912 to 1948, the Games held contests in five arts: architecture, literature, music, painting and sculpture.

slides.kicker: One rule: it had to be about sport.
slides.body:
Every entry had to be inspired by sport. Most had to be new, never published before.

Juries handed out gold, silver and bronze. When the work disappointed them, they could give no gold at all.

slides.kicker: The first gold went to two strangers.
slides.body:
In 1912, the literature gold went to "Ode to Sport", by Georges Hohrod and Martin Eschbach.

Neither man existed. The poem was written by Coubertin himself, under two fake names.
A shooter who sculpted, and a swimmer who designed a stadium.

In 1948, British artist John Copley won silver for an engraving of polo players.

He was 73. Some record books still call him the oldest Olympic medallist ever.

The Olympics were meant for amateurs. After 1948, the IOC concluded that almost all the artists were professionals, who lived from selling their work.

The contests were replaced by exhibitions. No medals, no podium.

slides.lead: Sometimes the rules meant to keep something pure
slides.accent: end up keeping out the best of it.

slides.line: Save this for the next time a rule forgets its purpose.

caption:
From 1912 to 1948, the Olympic Games awarded medals for painting, sculpture, music, literature and architecture. Founder Pierre de Coubertin even won gold for a poem, entered under two fake names. After 1948 the Olympic art competitions were dropped, because the artists were professionals.

Which art form would you bring back to the Olympics?
